In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
active replication is the best option in terms of end-to-end latency for a two-way remote method invocation, and semi-active replication is the best for a one-way remote method invocation.
the best end-to-end latency can be achieved with active replication, but only if an effective duplicate suppression mechanism is used.

the end-to-end latencies for active, semi-active, and passive replication are comparable, but the choice of the most appropriate replication strategy depends on the specific client and server invocation patterns.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the end-to-end performance of the infrastructure can be improved by carefully placing the primary replica, and by using active replication when possible.

the best end-to-end latency is obtained when the primary replica is located at the most favorable location on the ring and when the server processing time is short enough so that a single client invocation is completed during the token rotation interval.

, for active replication, the client invocation rate should be higher than the server processing time, for semi-active and active replication, the primary replica should be placed at the head of the ring, and for passive replication, the primary should be placed at a position such that the broadcast delay is minimized, which depends on the client invocation pattern and the server processing times.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the performance of a fault-tolerance protocol is not solely a function of the communication protocol used, but it is also dependent on the replication scheme and on the placement of the primary replica.

, in a CORBA infrastructure with a token-passing group-communication protocol, the end-to-end performance is highly dependent on the client invocation pattern and the server processing times, and that the position of the replica that is elected primary can have a significant effect on the end-to-end latencies seen by the client.
the end-to-end performance of a replicated system is not just a function of the communication protocol, but also of the replication scheme.
